toc.title: Crying as the release of freeze
When crying doesn't get you anywhere

blocks.p: The freeze mixed state can have a regulated release and a dysregulated release. I want to make sure you can spot the difference. This comes from a letter one listener sent me about crying, freeze, and what happens when the release doesn't go well.

q: Hey, Justin. I hope you're doing great. I wanted to reach out to you to ask you one question about the freeze state. I know from my personal experience that the freeze state does not allow for crying. My home away from home is the sympathetic flight-fight defensive response. Whenever I get triggered, I automatically go into a freeze state and have no access to crying. It's frustrating because I feel I need to cry to discharge the defensive energy, but I am not able to do it at a biological level.

What ends up happening to me is that I begin to experience this urge to bang my head or scream or run away, but I can't. I'm pretty sure this is the way my body aims to release the defensive energy that keeps building up, but obviously acting on these urges can do me more harm.

My question is, why is it, or what happens at a biological level, when you are not able to discharge that frozen energy with a cry? My hypothesis is that whenever I have a biological access to crying, I come down the ladder to a dorsal state. My experience in this state is more of a relief, because even though this crying can become uncontrollable and I often hyperventilate, when it stops, I feel discharged.

blocks.p: There are a few things in here I want to highlight, especially the self-harm piece, and how it connects to freeze and to the dysregulated version of trying to discharge it.

I agree that when someone is actively in a freeze state, crying probably isn't going to happen. Probably not. But coming out of freeze could involve crying, and I think it's pretty darn likely that it would. I don't think it has to, but I think it's likely.

First, a reminder that freeze and shutdown are different. I covered this in episodes 101 through 109. Shutdown is that limp, immobilized collapse. Freeze is that tense immobilization. Freeze is a mixed state of the Polyvagal Theory, not a primary state. It's not just a so-called trauma response. It is the sympathetic flight-fight state active along with the dorsal vagal shutdown state. Flight-fight plus shutdown. That's freeze.
Each polyvagal state has an impulse or two or more associated with it, meaning there's something the body wants to do. The body is primed to do something based on the state it's in.

That includes the safety state. In your ventral vagal state of safety and social engagement, the impulse is to connect with others. More specifically, it could be to hug somebody, to smile or laugh, or to make gentle eye contact.

It includes freeze too. For freeze, the impulse seems to me to be tensing and releasing. It's like you're bracing for impact. I don't think freeze is just a glitch in the system where you're paralyzed in the moment, frozen in fear. I think it has an evolutionary benefit. Being frozen in fear could increase survivability. It could even mimic a corpse. That's not really an impulse, but it's an evolutionary benefit.
As far as the impulse goes, freeze is like tensing in anticipation or preparation of explosion. That might be an explosion into aggression, or an explosion into escape, running away.

So I think freeze has a different flavor based on which sympathetic state is active along with the immobilization. There's a freeze sort of anger, and a freeze sort of flight, anxious flight. Immobilization active along with flight is a different experience from immobilization active along with fight. Both are sympathetic, but combined with immobilization, they can look different, feel different, and behave differently. The impulses that come with them will be different as well.
In general, though, freeze carries an impulse to brace and then explode in flight or fight: to escape or to use aggression.

blocks.h: Crying as the release of freeze

blocks.p: For us humans, on a more day-to-day basis, I think the more common release is crying. I think crying is the release of the freeze state.

You may know Peter Levine's famous polar bear video. The polar bear is tranquilized while it's running away from people in a helicopter. While it's tranquilized, it's immobilized, but the flight energy, maybe some fight too, is trapped in its system. When it comes out of that state, it has to shake and tremble the potential trauma off. In the video, they describe it as the polar bear releasing the stress, but really it's flight energy. The bear naturally knows how to self-regulate: it shakes and trembles and breathes spontaneously and discharges the stuck flight energy.

We humans can do that. It doesn't seem as natural for us anymore, but we can, and I think our version of it is crying. Think about how, when we cry, we shake and tremble and shudder, and we have this spontaneous breathing. And when we're done crying, a lot of times we feel better. Not every time, but we feel different. We might feel lighter. We might feel more able to connect. We might feel more in our safety state after crying out whatever sympathetic energy was stuck inside us.
So crying and freeze go hand in hand, but I'd say it's more about coming out of freeze and crying it out.

Coming out of shutdown is different. I don't want to speak in absolutes, but usually what I see is that people don't really cry as they come out of shutdown. They have a surge, or a gradual surge, of fight energy as they climb their ladder. Freeze seems to have crying associated with it.

You might be reading this and saying, "Cool. But I can't cry. It doesn't come out." A lot of my clients say they don't cry, or can't cry, in front of others. I believe them. I see it in session: they might have an impulse to cry, but it doesn't come out. The impulse is there, but it's not acted on.

I think it's pretty common to feel embarrassment or vulnerability when we cry in front of others. If we cried in front of others in the past and got negative reactions, humiliation, or ridicule, that could have been its own little trauma. So of course you're not going to want to cry in front of somebody because of that past event or events.

But also, as you come up the polyvagal ladder into your safety state, as you get more self-regulated and grounded, being in your safety state in front of someone else might feel really uncomfortable. You have to be able to tolerate that discomfort, and that can be a big challenge. So your ability to cry in front of somebody else, even a therapist, or a spouse, a loved one, or a friend, might be less. It's uncomfortable. Vulnerability is a challenge, and that's okay.

blocks.h: When crying doesn't get you anywhere

blocks.p: Or maybe you're someone who cries a ton and it doesn't get you anywhere. I've met with those people as well. Maybe you can't stop crying, or when you cry, it turns into something else, like panic or destruction. Maybe it's completely overwhelming.

That's different from what I just described. When it's uncomfortable to cry in front of someone, or uncomfortable to feel these feelings, there's more regulation in there. It's just uncomfortable and vulnerable.

What I'm describing now is a dysregulated attempt at freeze release. The body is trying to discharge its stuck freeze energy, but there's not enough safety in the system to even notice that it's uncomfortable, or maybe even to notice an impulse to cry and be vulnerable, if there is one at all.

When the safety state is active, freeze can result in crying that can be felt, experienced, and discharged successfully. Maybe not all at once, but gradually, over time, there can be a successful discharge.

Dysregulated freeze might result in some crying, but it would be an uncontrollable, unproductive cry. It would feel overwhelming. Dysregulated freeze discharging, or attempting to discharge, can also look like rage or panic.

Dysregulation here means there isn't enough safety active in the system to tolerate it. The vagal brake isn't active, or it isn't strong enough. So the defensive state is too much. There's too much flight-fight in the system, too much freeze, and not enough safety.

If there's too much fight and immobilization and it gets triggered, that could result in explosive rage. Remember the tensing and then releasing impulse. Someone stuck in an angry, immobilized fight state might have rage inside them that just lingers all the time. When it gets triggered, it explodes. It makes me wonder about people who are abusive, and why the rage comes up around someone their body detects as weaker than them. Could that be a faulty neuroception, not of safety, but of a perceived lack of danger? I wonder.
Panic is also freeze, but more of the flight variety. There's anxiety in panic. Rage is more anger, fight. Panic is more anxiety, flight. Both come with the immobilization.

Someone could be triggered into freeze. Or the freeze energy could be attempting to discharge, and the person can't handle it. They can't tolerate the amount of flight-fight in their system, and they also can't work through the immobilization. I think you have to work through the immobilization first and then work on the flight-fight. That's typically how I go about it.

This panic, rage, overwhelm, or uncontrollable, unproductive crying is out of control. It's explosive. It's mindless rather than mindful, and that's not a dig or an insult. It just means the person isn't able to be in their safety state while witnessing and experiencing the stuck state. That's fine. I don't expect them to. It's a lot.
This could eventually lead to what the letter writer described about self-harm.

I think a lot of different things can bring somebody to self-harm, including intense self-hatred, though I'd say that's more of a freeze. It might be a relief from whatever they're going through. It might be a distraction, a physical distraction. There could be a lot of different paths that lead someone there, and a lot of different temporary pseudo benefits they could get from it.
Self-harm is a behavioral adaptation. It feels a bit better in the moment. It feels less crummy. But it's obviously not effective, and it could end up making things worse.

What I've noticed is that there definitely tends to be a freeze aspect to self-harm, one that can feel more like panic or rage. I think self-hatred could be a form of rage as well. It could be overwhelm, so much inner turmoil that the physical aspect of self-harm might be a relief. I think a lot of that stems from dysregulated freeze.

As I break this down with my clients and we look at the self-harm thoughts and do a chain analysis of how they got to that point, a lot of times it's this freeze energy attempting to come out and discharge, and they can't handle it. That's okay, for now. I can't tell you what your freeze state is like or what your self-harm is there for. I'm not saying that. But for the clients I work with in therapy, this seems to be a repeated pattern: the freeze state is triggered and attempting to discharge, and the self-harm plays a role in alleviating that temporarily.
To get actual relief from all of this, I'm going to implore you to develop the strength of your vagal brake, your safety state. I'm going to beg you to work on the strength of your safety state.

It's not easy, I know. But instead of delving into the trauma narrative, instead of attempting to feel all of your feelings, instead of meditating on the pain you're in for an hour or two or three, why not use that time to do something that helps you ground in safety?

Grounding in safety is the absolute priority when it comes to trauma relief. Once you're grounded in safety, you can start to work on the defensive state: the freeze, the flight and fight. Once you're grounded in safety, you can have a more productive cry, or two, or three, or four, a mindful cry, and get some actual relief and do some discharging.
This is a lot, and I don't expect you to take it and run with it right away. I hope it brings some clarity.

blocks.why: This article talks about mindfulness. This practice gives you a few minutes of it.
